topics.title: Form Validation by Hand
topics.summary: Validate on blur and submit, keep errors in state, and show messages next to the fields.
topics.description:
Before reaching for a library, understand the manual approach. A validation flow has four parts.

### 1. Values and errors in state

Keep `values` (what the user typed), `errors` (messages by field name) and `touched` (fields the user has left) in state.

### 2. A pure `validate(values)` function

It returns an object like `{ email: "Invalid email" }`. Pure functions are easy to unit test and reuse on server and client.

### 3. When to validate

- **On submit** - always block the submit if there are errors.
- **On blur** - show an error when the user leaves a field (use `touched`) so you do not shout while they are still typing.
- **On change** - for fields that have been touched or already show an error, to clear the message as soon as it is fixed.

### 4. Accessible feedback

Link each error to its input with `aria-describedby`, set `aria-invalid`, move focus to the first invalid field on failed submit, and use `role="alert"` for dynamic messages.

### Client vs server validation

Client validation is for UX. **Never trust it for security**: the server must validate again, and it can return field errors that you map into the same `errors` state.

### When it gets heavy

Many fields, arrays, async checks and dependent fields quickly become repetitive. That is when React Hook Form and a schema library like Zod are worth it.
keyPoints: Keep values, errors and touched in state
Write validation as a pure function
Validate on blur and submit; clear errors on change
Use aria-invalid and aria-describedby for accessibility
Always validate again on the server
pitfalls: Showing errors before the user touched the field.
Validating only in the UI and trusting the data on the server.

examples.title: Sign-up form with touched + submit validation

interview.q: When should you show validation errors?
interview.a: After the user has interacted with the field (blur/touched) or tried to submit, not while they have not started typing.

interview.q: Why is client-side validation not enough?
interview.a: Users can bypass the browser, so the server must validate again for security and data integrity.

topics.title: React Hook Form
topics.summary: React Hook Form manages forms with minimal re-renders using uncontrolled inputs and a simple register API.
topics.description:
**React Hook Form (RHF)** is the most popular form library. It mostly uses **uncontrolled inputs** and refs under the hood, so typing in one field does not re-render the whole form. It also gives validation, error state, dirty/touched tracking and easy integration with schema validators.

### Core API

| API | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `useForm()` | creates the form instance |
| `register("name", rules)` | connects an input; returns `ref`, `name`, `onChange`, `onBlur` |
| `handleSubmit(fn)` | validates, then calls `fn(data)` |
| `formState.errors` | validation errors per field |
| `formState.isSubmitting`, `isDirty`, `isValid` | status flags |
| `watch("field")` | subscribe to value changes (causes re-render) |
| `reset()`, `setValue()`, `getValues()` | imperative control |
| `Controller` / `useController` | integrate controlled UI libs (MUI, Select) |
| `useFieldArray` | dynamic lists of inputs |

### Rules

Built-in rules: `required`, `min`, `max`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern`, `validate` (custom function, can be async).

### Why teams like it

- Very small bundle, no dependencies.
- Few re-renders - great for big forms.
- Works with TypeScript (typed form values).
- Pairs with `@hookform/resolvers` for Zod/Yup.

### Modes

`mode: "onSubmit"` (default), `"onBlur"`, `"onChange"`, `"onTouched"` decide when validation runs.

### Tips

Provide `defaultValues` for every field, use `Controller` for non-native inputs, and prefer `watch` sparingly.
keyPoints: useForm + register connects inputs without state
handleSubmit validates then passes data
formState.errors holds messages
Few re-renders thanks to uncontrolled inputs
Controller for custom components; useFieldArray for lists
pitfalls: Forgetting defaultValues, leading to undefined values and warnings.
Overusing watch(), which re-renders on each change.

examples.title: React Hook Form sign-up

interview.q: Why is React Hook Form fast?
interview.a: It relies on uncontrolled inputs and refs, so typing does not trigger a re-render of the whole form on every keystroke.
An object with name, ref, onChange and onBlur handlers that you spread onto the input to connect it to the form.

topics.title: Schema Validation with Zod
topics.summary: Describe your data shape once with Zod, and reuse it for validation and TypeScript types.
topics.description:
**Zod** is a TypeScript-first schema library. You define a schema describing valid data, then parse input with it. The same schema gives you runtime validation **and** a static TypeScript type via `z.infer`.

```js
import { z } from "zod";

const signUpSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email("Invalid email"),
  password: z.string().min(8, "Min 8 chars"),
  confirm: z.string(),
  age: z.coerce.number().int().min(18, "Must be 18+"),
}).refine(d => d.password === d.confirm, {
  message: "Passwords do not match",
  path: ["confirm"],
});
```

### Parsing

- `schema.parse(data)` returns typed data or throws `ZodError`.
- `schema.safeParse(data)` returns `{ success, data | error }` without throwing.
- `error.flatten().fieldErrors` gives messages per field.

### Common building blocks

`z.string()`, `z.number()`, `z.boolean()`, `z.date()`, `z.enum([...])`, `z.array()`, `z.object()`, `.optional()`, `.nullable()`, `.default()`, `.transform()`, `.refine()`, `z.coerce.number()` (form values are strings!), `z.infer<typeof schema>`.

### With React Hook Form

Install `@hookform/resolvers` and pass `resolver: zodResolver(schema)` to `useForm`. Errors then flow into `formState.errors` automatically.

### Share between client and server

Put the schema in a shared package. The API validates incoming bodies with the very same schema, so rules never drift. Alternatives: Yup, Valibot, ArkType.
keyPoints: Schema = single source of truth for validation and types
safeParse avoids exceptions
z.coerce converts form strings to numbers/dates
refine adds cross-field rules
zodResolver connects Zod to React Hook Form
pitfalls: Forgetting that form inputs return strings; numbers need z.coerce.number().
Putting cross-field errors on the wrong path.

examples.title: Zod + React Hook Form
safeParse on the server

interview.a: A TypeScript type derived from the schema, so the runtime validation and compile-time types always match.

interview.q: Why use z.coerce for form values?
interview.a: HTML inputs always give strings; coerce converts them to numbers or dates before validating.

topics.title: File Upload and Preview
topics.summary: Read the selected file from an input, validate its type and size, preview it, and send it with FormData.
topics.description:
A file input is always **uncontrolled** in React; you cannot set its value. You read the selected files from `e.target.files` (a `FileList`) in the `onChange` handler.

### Steps

1. Render `<input type="file" accept="image/*" />` (add `multiple` for many files).
2. In `onChange`, take `e.target.files[0]`.
3. **Validate** `file.type` and `file.size` on the client (limits are for UX; the server must check again).
4. **Preview** images with `URL.createObjectURL(file)` and **revoke** the URL when done (cleanup) to avoid memory leaks. Alternatively use `FileReader.readAsDataURL`.
5. **Upload** with `FormData`:

```js
const fd = new FormData();
fd.append("avatar", file);
await fetch("/api/upload", { method: "POST", body: fd });
```

Do **not** set the `Content-Type` header yourself; the browser adds the multipart boundary.

### Progress

`fetch` has no upload progress. Use `XMLHttpRequest` (`xhr.upload.onprogress`) or axios `onUploadProgress`.

### Large files and production

Use **pre-signed URLs** (S3/GCS) so the browser uploads directly to storage, chunked/resumable uploads (tus), and drag-and-drop zones (`react-dropzone`). Always scan and validate on the server; never trust the file extension or MIME type sent by the client.
keyPoints: e.target.files holds selected files
File inputs are uncontrolled
Preview with createObjectURL and revoke on cleanup
Upload with FormData; do not set Content-Type manually
Server must re-validate type and size
pitfalls: Manually setting the multipart Content-Type header, breaking the boundary.

examples.title: Pick a file, validate and show details
examples.explanation: In a real app you would send the file via FormData.

interview.q: How do you upload a file from React?
interview.a: Read it from the input's files, append it to a FormData object and send with fetch or axios as the request body; the browser sets the multipart header.
createObjectURL keeps the file in memory until it is revoked, so cleaning up avoids memory leaks.

topics.title: Accessibility (a11y) in React
topics.summary: Use semantic HTML, labels, keyboard support, focus management and ARIA so everyone can use your app.
topics.description:
Accessibility means people using screen readers, keyboards, voice control or with low vision can use your UI. React renders ordinary HTML, so the same rules apply, with a few React-specific tools.

### The most important rules

1. **Semantic HTML first:** use `button`, `a`, `nav`, `main`, `ul`, `label`, headings in order. A clickable `<div>` has no keyboard support or role.
2. **Labels:** every input needs a `<label htmlFor>` (or `aria-label`). Use `useId` for unique ids.
3. **Keyboard:** everything clickable must be reachable with Tab and operable with Enter/Space. Never remove focus outlines without a replacement.
4. **Alt text:** meaningful `alt` for images; `alt=""` for decorative ones.
5. **Color contrast:** at least 4.5:1 for body text.
6. **Announce changes:** `role="alert"` or `aria-live="polite"` for toasts, errors and async results.

### React-specific tips

- Use **Fragments** to keep valid HTML structure (table rows, lists).
- `htmlFor`, `tabIndex`, `aria-*` and `role` are written as camelCase/lowercase attributes in JSX.
- **Manage focus** with refs when UI changes: move focus into a modal, back to the trigger on close, and to the new heading after a route change.
- Use `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` to catch problems at build time.
- Test with the keyboard, a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver), axe DevTools and Lighthouse; `jest-axe` in unit tests.

### ARIA rule of thumb

*No ARIA is better than bad ARIA.* Use ARIA only when HTML cannot express the widget (tabs, combobox), and implement the full keyboard pattern.
keyPoints: Prefer semantic HTML over div soup with ARIA
Every control needs a label and keyboard access
Manage focus for modals and route changes
Use aria-live for dynamic messages
Lint with jsx-a11y and test with axe and keyboard
pitfalls: Using div or span with onClick instead of a button.
Removing outline: none without a custom focus style.
Using placeholder as the only label.

examples.title: Accessible toggle with live status

interview.q: Why use a button instead of a clickable div?
interview.a: A button is focusable, activates with Enter/Space and exposes the correct role to assistive tech; a div has none of that by default.

interview.q: How do you announce dynamic content to screen readers?
interview.a: Render it in an element with aria-live (for example role="status" or role="alert") so changes are read out.
